query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The naturally-grown oxide film on as-received Q235 steel passivates the surface at room temperature to suppress corrosion, but when exposed at elevated temperatures, thermal stresses induce cracking and delamination of the oxide film, thereby exposing the substrate to aggressive environments and accelerating corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its typical as-received (pre-exposure) state with its native, naturally-formed surface oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A controlled surface treatment that removes the native oxide layer (e.g., via mechanical polishing) followed by re-oxidation under carefully controlled conditions to create a uniform and adherent oxide film, compared with samples retaining their initial oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Exposure to harsh corrosive environments (such as saline or acidic solutions) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (for example, around 80°C) to evaluate temperature‐dependent changes in corrosion behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity, microstructure, and adhesion quality of the surface oxide film on Q235 steel.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, a stable and uniform oxide film limits oxygen and ion ingress, acting as a barrier to corrosion. When exposed to elevated temperatures, thermal expansion differences induce mechanical stresses that lead to crack formation and delamination of the oxide film. This breakdown exposes fresh metal, which accelerates localized corrosion mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that retain a defect-free, adherent oxide film are predicted to exhibit lower corrosion rates at room temperature compared to samples where the film suffers cracking at elevated temperatures. With increasing temperature, samples with compromised oxide films are expected to show accelerated corrosion relative to untreated or better-controlled re-oxidized samples.
generation.baseline: The untreated Q235 steel with its native oxide film in its initial, as-received state tested under the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under corrosive conditions without significant mechanical damage to the substrate and assumes that alloying elements are at levels typical for Q235 steel. Variations in environmental aggressiveness or deviations in intrinsic alloy composition might affect the results.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise microstructural evolution and phase changes of the oxide film at elevated temperatures, as well as the quantitative relationship between film degradation and corrosion rate acceleration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples. One set retains the native oxide film (untreated), while the other set is mechanically polished to remove the oxide film and then re-oxidized under controlled conditions to produce a uniform and adherent oxide layer. Expose both sets to a harsh corrosive solution (e.g., sodium chloride solution, possibly adjusted to acidic pH) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (around 80°C). Monitor the evolution of the oxide layer and surface condition using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, and adhesion/crack tests. Measure corrosion rates using weight loss measurements and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for quantitative assessment.
measurements: Corrosion rate (via weight loss and/or EIS)
Oxide film integrity and microstructure (SEM imaging, XRD phase analysis)
Mechanical integrity of the oxide film (adhesion and crack density evaluation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed at elevated temperatures do not show increased film cracking/delamination and no corresponding acceleration in corrosion rate (compared with room temperature results) relative to the untreated references, then the hypothesis that thermal destabilization of the oxide film drives accelerated corrosion will be falsified.
